What if you could install your own personal AI agent directly on your laptop and connect it to your everyday workflows? 

The world of AI agents is evolving rapidly, with tools like ChatGPT, Claude Code, Codex, and n8n changing how we automate tasks and build AI-powered applications.

Now, another open-source personal AI agent is entering the conversation!

In this video, I'll explore this new AI agent, explain its capabilities, and walk you through the process of installing and setting it up on your laptop.

 Why Personal AI Agents Matter

Traditional AI chatbots primarily respond to your questions and prompts.

Personal AI agents can go further by combining AI models with tools, integrations, memory, and task execution capabilities.

Depending on their configuration, they may help with research, file management, coding, planning, and repetitive workflows.

Open-source projects also give developers opportunities to inspect the implementation, customize workflows, and experiment with self-hosted setups.

From n8n Automation to Personal AI Agents

If you've been following my channel, you know we've explored n8n, AI automation, Claude Code, and other agentic AI tools.

This tutorial continues that journey by exploring a new personal AI agent and its potential role in your AI workflow.

We'll focus on the installation process, available integrations, and practical ways to get started.

Important: Open-source doesn't always mean completely free to operate. Some integrations and AI models may require API keys or paid services. Review the agent's permissions before granting access to personal files or accounts.

Who Should Watch?

• n8n users and automation builders

• AI developers and enthusiasts

• Claude Code and Codex users

• Students exploring agentic AI

• Anyone interested in open-source personal AI assistants

videos.title: 2-NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails Tutorial: Defend RAG Apps Against Prompt Injection | Part 1
videos.description:
Code: https://github.com/krishnaik06/Ai-Safety-And-LLM-Security
Learn how to add NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails to a RAG application and test defenses against direct prompt injection, poisoned documents, and unsafe responses.

In this hands-on tutorial, we configure input, document/retrieval, and output checks, then integrate them into a LangGraph workflow. Using an example company help assistant, we compare the application’s behavior before and after adding guardrails.

You’ll see how policy-based checks can block off-topic instructions, filter suspicious retrieved passages, and inspect generated answers. We also test normal questions to check whether the guarded application still provides useful responses.

This is Part 1 of the NeMo Guardrails walkthrough, combining architecture explanations, Python implementation, and practical attack testing.

⏱️ TIMESTAMPS & TOPICS

00:00 Introduction and recap of prompt injection attacks
00:50 What is NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails?
01:30 Tutorial roadmap and guardrail categories
02:46 What are rails? Understanding policy-based checks
04:44 Where input, retrieval, and output rails fit in RAG
06:28 Python dependencies, imports, and RailStatus
07:53 Project structure and NeMo configuration files
09:20 Configuring self-check input policies
10:26 Configuring self-check output policies
12:19 Document rail configuration
13:05 Retrieval rails: checking context before generation
14:35 Loading configurations with LLMRails
15:06 Testing input rails with allowed and blocked questions
16:39 Testing document rails with clean and poisoned passages
17:43 Testing output rails with safe and damaging answers
18:37 Building a guarded RAG workflow with LangGraph
20:36 Preparing direct and indirect attack examples
21:16 Creating clean and poisoned vector stores
21:56 Direct prompt injection: before vs after guardrails
23:51 Indirect prompt injection and poisoned-document results
24:47 Comparing results in the attack scoreboard
25:12 Testing normal questions and checking false positives
25:58 Summary and what’s coming in Part 2  

💡 WHAT YOU’LL LEARN
- How programmable guardrails fit around an LLM application.
- How to define policies in config.yml.
- How to configure self_check_input and self_check_output.
- How to load configurations using RailsConfig and LLMRails.
- How to run asynchronous checks and inspect their status.
- How to filter retrieved documents before passing context to the LLM.
- How to connect input checks, retrieval, document checks, generation, and output checks in LangGraph.
- How to compare guarded and unguarded applications using the same test cases.
- How to check that legitimate user questions still work.
